justification: This clears the top-ranking results for '.net garbage collector explained' by a wide margin and is close to the 10 anchor. The official Microsoft Learn fundamentals page (the highest-authority result) states every fact this article states, but never once demonstrates any of it with running code and never mentions the practical leak scenarios (a static cache with no eviction, an event subscription that outlives its subscriber) that are this article's stated angle in CONTENT_PLAN.md section 7 ('Leak demos you can run; disposal vs collection disentangled'); I fetched that page directly and confirmed the article's quotations from it ('it's faster to compact the memory for a portion...', 'newer objects have shorter lifetimes...', the roots list, the compaction-is-conditional sentence) are verbatim-accurate and used exactly where the source supports them. The two representative blog-tier results I fetched (techsyntax.net, whose title is close to the exact target query, and blog.elmah.io) both show code with no real execution output and cite no primary sources at all, which is exactly the 'decent personal blog, anchor 7' tier; this article runs every example and shows the actual result, with volatile machine-dependent numbers correctly wildcarded (`[...]`) per the site's own hard rule 2, while deterministic ones (the 84,976-byte LOH boundary, the 500/0 and 250/500 leak-fix counts) are left as exact reproducible values. The two leak demonstrations (permanent-root static cache, event-handler leak fixed with `using`+unsubscribe) are original constructions built for this article, not reused from any cited source, and the reachability, generation-promotion, LOH-boundary and mark/compact diagrams are all original SVGs with distinct captions. I web-searched five distinctive sentences from the article in quotes ('Two objects can hold references to each other and still both be garbage...', 'Forty bytes of array length is the entire difference...', plus a paraphrase check on the finalization-queue and static-cache passages); none returned a matching or closely paraphrased source, and the search budget was exhausted before the fifth check completed, but nothing found in the completed checks suggests copying. Structurally the article avoids every pilot-round failure mode: no filler intro ('A .NET program never calls `free`' delivers content in its first clause), no boilerplate 'Introduction'/'Conclusion' headings, the closing section is a question ('How do you check any of this without guessing?') rather than a restated-heading summary, every one of the eleven front-matter sources is cited inline at the point of the claim it supports (none orphaned), and — unlike this same pillar's sibling article in its own round 1 — none of the six exercises leaks its output ahead of the solution: the two 'Predict it' exercises correctly withhold the output block until inside `:::solution`, and the two 'Find the bug' exercises correctly show output as part of the puzzle itself (a different, legitimate exercise shape), which is the distinction the editorial brief draws. Compared against the published sibling `value-types-vs-reference-types.md` and against `four-pillars-of-oop.md` (also shape Q), the heading style, diagram conventions and exercise/solution markup are consistent with the site's design system but the headings, examples (invoices/plans vs. sensors/gauges/tanks) and phrasing are not reused or templated between articles — this reads as the same author's consistent voice, not machine-generated boilerplate. Two minor issues keep it below a 9.5+: an unscoped absolute claim in the opening line, and repeated exercise-label shapes within the same article.

issues.location: Opening paragraph, first sentence: "A .NET program never calls `free`."
issues.problem: The editorial brief's binding 'Lessons from the pilot round' warns that absolute words (only/always/never/entire/every) get checked and have already cost earlier articles their pass. Taken literally, a .NET program can call `free`-equivalent functions: this very article's own `SensorProbe`/`Gauge` examples later call `Marshal.FreeHGlobal`, and P/Invoke can call the C runtime `free` directly. The sentence is clearly meant to mean 'on the managed heap,' but as written it is an unscoped absolute in the load-bearing first sentence of the article.
issues.fixLooksLike: Scope the claim, e.g. "A .NET program never calls `free` to release a managed object" or "Nothing in ordinary C# calls `free`", so the later unmanaged-memory sections (which do call `Marshal.FreeHGlobal`) don't read as contradicting the opening hook.

issues.location: Exercise headings throughout the article: 'Predict it: which weak reference survives' / 'Predict it: partial cleanup' (both predict-the-output), and 'Find the bug' / 'Find the bug: a check that always passes' (both find-the-bug)
issues.problem: Of the six exercises, two forms are each used twice (predict-the-output, find-the-bug) while 'prove-it' is never used; the brief's binding pilot-round lessons call for varying exercise form across an article, and the recurring identical opening words ('Predict it', 'Find the bug') on two exercises each read as a mini-template inside a single page, which is exactly the kind of repetition an AdSense-style low-value-content check looks for even though each individual exercise's content is original.
issues.fixLooksLike: Reshape one of the two 'Find the bug' exercises (the second one, on `WeakReference.IsAlive`, fits naturally) into a 'prove-it' form — e.g. 'prove that no collection happened between adding the item and reading IsAlive' — so no exercise label is reused verbatim within the page.
